                         MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
 1

 2           Pursuant to Civil Local Rule 11-5 and in compliance with California Rules of

 3   Professional Conduct 1.16(b)(4) and (5), all attorneys of the Moya Law Firm (“MLF”) hereby
     move for withdrawal as counsel for Defendant/ Counterclaimant/ Cross-Claimant/ and
 4
     Third-Party Plaintiff Dasagroup Holdings Corp. in this action. This motion is based on the
 5
     accompanying Declaration of Mario A. Moya (“Moya Decl.”) in support of this motion.
 6
       I.​   BACKGROUND
 7
                A.​ Procedural History
 8
             Since being retained in this case, MLF has diligently and zealously represented
 9
     Dasagroup’s rights and interests in accordance with all applicable professional obligations. On
10
     November 4, 2024, Dasagroup filed an Answer and Counterclaims (Dkt. No. 11) against plaintiff
11
     Jefferies Funding, LLC for (1) declaratory relief; (2) unjust enrichment re: MSA & Forbearance
12
     Agreement; (3) rescission; (4) breach of covenant of good faith and fair dealing (5) common
13   count - money had and received; (6) unfair/unlawful business practices, in addition to cross
14   claims against defendant London Fruit for (7) breach of contract; (8) account stated; and (9)
15   unjust enrichment. See Dkt. No. 11. This filing was subsequently amended without leave, with
16   minor amendments, on Nov. 22, 2024. See Dkt. No. 28. On Nov. 18, 2024, Dasagroup filed a
17   third-party complaint to add Silo Technologies, Inc. (“Silo”) as a third-party defendant to the
18   action. See Dkt. No. 23. Jefferies and Silo filed motions to dismiss the amended counterclaims

19   and third-party complaint, respectively. See Dkt. Nos. 33, 51. The Court granted in part and

20   denied in part the motions to dismiss, with leave to amend. Dkt. No. 72.

21           Following motion practice, in March 2025, Dasagroup filed a Second Amended Answer

22   and Counterclaim against Jefferies and a First Amended Third Party Complaint against Silo. See
     Dkt. No. 78, 79. Jefferies and Silo filed a joint motion to dismiss, which the Court granted in
23
     part and denied in part on June 16, 2025. See Dkt. Nos. 85, 99. Dasagroup subsequently filed
24
     its Third Amended Answer and Counterclaim and Second Amended Third Party Complaint with
25
     narrowed claims following orders on dispositive motions. See Dkt. Nos. 101, 102. Jefferies and
26
     Silo ultimately filed their respective answers on July 14, 2025. Dkt. Nos. 111-112.
27
28

            On Aug. 6, 2025 Jefferies filed a First Amended Complaint (FAC) adding Mr. Ward as an
 1
     additional defendant to the action and asserting new claims under California Penal Code Section
 2
     496(c). Dkt. No. 122. In response, Dasagroup filed a motion to dismiss the FAC, and, in
 3
     particular, the claim for treble damages under California Penal Code Section 496 on Aug. 20,
 4
     2025. Dkt. No. 133.
 5
            On Sept. 4, 2025, Jefferies filed an administrative motion for an order allowing
 6
     alternative service on Mr. Ward, seeking to serve Mr. Ward by, among other things, service on
 7
     the Moya Law Firm as counsel for Dasagroup. See Dkt. No. 138. The undersigned counsel
 8
     filed an opposition to the administrative motion, clarifying that counsel for Dasagroup was not
 9   authorized to accept service on behalf of Mr. Ward individually and that the Moya Law Firm had
10   not been retained to represent Mr. Ward in his individual capacity. See Dkt. No. 139. On Sept.
11   10, 2025, the Court entered an Order granting as modified Jefferies’s administrative motion, but
12   excluded service on the Moya Law Firm as an option for service of Mr. Ward. Dkt. No. 141.
13   Following the Court’s order, counsel for Jefferies has informed the undersigned counsel that it
14   has taken steps to effectuate service on Mr. Ward, but no proof of service has yet to be filed.

15          Trial date is set in this case for January 4, 2027. See Dkt. No. 29. The Court’s

16   most-recent case management and scheduling order was entered on Aug. 22, 2025. Dkt. No.

17   129, 136. The close of fact discovery is currently set for Nov. 30, 2025. See Dkt. 129. The

18   parties have engaged in significant discovery in this case. To date, Dasagroup has produced
     17,060 pages of documents in this case over the course of 8 productions. Moya Decl. 10. In
19
     addition, Dasagroup has responded to seven sets of written discovery from Jefferies and Silo,
20
     including a combined 42 requests for production, 47 interrogatories, and 66 requests for
21
     admissions. Id.
22
            To date, only one deposition has taken place (of defaulted Defendant London Fruit’s
23
     corporate representative), and the deposition of third-party Kitzia Lauren Huerta (Mr. Ward’s
24
     wife) has been recently set for October 17, 2025. Id. No other depositions are currently set. Id.
25
                B.​ Grounds for Withdrawal & Avoidance of Prejudice
26
            The Moya Law Firm has represented Dasagroup Holdings Corp. since last year. See
27
     Moya Decl. 4. As noted in the accompanying declaration of counsel, there has recently been
28
        NTC. OF MOT. TO WITHDRAW AS COUNSEL FOR DASAGROUP WITH MEMORANDUM
                                                      4          Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                 No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 147        Filed 09/17/25         Page 5 of 10


     an irreparable breakdown in the attorney-client relationship between Dasagroup and MLF such
 1
     that the firm cannot continue to effectively represent Dasagroup in connection with this matter.
 2
     Moya Decl. ¶¶ 18-19. In addition — and unrelated to the breakdown in the attorney-client
 3
     relationship — Dasagroup has materially breached its representation agreement with MLF. See
 4
     id. ¶¶ 11-16. This breach has placed a significant financial burden on MLF, which will be
 5
     exacerbated if this motion to withdraw is not granted. Id. 17.
 6
            Professional considerations require withdrawal. Counsel has provided Dasagroup with
 7
     written notice of their intent to withdraw, as required by Local Rule 11-5(a), in correspondence
 8
     sent on July 29, 2025; August 22, 2025; Sept. 15, 2025; and today, Sept. 16, 2025, with an
 9   additional copy of this motion — noticed for hearing on Nov. 11 — being served via email and
10   U.S. mail. See Moya Decl. ¶¶ 20-22. Counsel for Jefferies and Silo was provided notice of
11   counsel’s intent to withdraw orally on Sept. 15, 2025. Id. 24. On behalf of Dasagroup, counsel
12   seeks a 60-day continuance of all pending deadlines to allow for substitution of counsel.
13          The undersigned counsel has taken reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable prejudice to
14   Dasagroup and others resulting from any anticipated withdrawal. The undersigned counsel has

15   filed a motion to dismiss the First Amended Complaint filed against Dasagroup challenging the

16   standing and justiciability of original Jefferies’s lawsuit (which the FAC and other

17   recently-discovered state UCC filings made readily apparent), in addition to a

18   statute-of-limitations challenge to a new third claim for relief asserted under Penal Code
     § 496(c). See Moya Decl. ¶¶ 9, 21. That motion presents a narrow issue of standing that is
19
     largely unaddressed by prior case law on similar facts to this case — i.e., whether UCC 9-607
20
     (i.e., Cal. Commercial Code § 9607) confers sufficient standing for a secured party to sue a
21
     defendant on behalf of a third-party debtor. For reasons briefed in that motion, there is no
22
     Article III standing on the facts originally pleaded by Jefferies, and such issues cannot be waived
23
     under the Federal Rules and binding authority from the Supreme Court.
24
            By this motion to withdraw, which is set for hearing on Nov. 11, 2025 (which is the
25
     earliest date available per the Court’s online calendar), counsel asks the Court to stay any
26
     pending litigation deadlines until the company is able to secure new counsel. In the meantime, I
27
28

                                                      5          Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                 No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
         Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 147         Filed 09/17/25         Page 6 of 10


     have informed my client that I would be willing to provide interim assistance to comply with
 1
     Magistrate Judge Ryu’s recent ADR order, which was entered just yesterday. See ECF 144.
 2
      II.​   ARGUMENT
 3
                A.​ Standard of Review
 4
             Under Civil Local Rule 11-5(a), counsel “may not withdraw from an action until relieved
 5
     by order of the Court after written notice has been provided, reasonably in advance, to the client
 6
     and to all other parties who have appeared in the case.” N.D.Cal. Civ. L.R. 11-5(a). The
 7
     California Rules of Professional Conduct apply to requests to withdraw as counsel of record. See
 8
     Civ. L.R. 11-4; Nehad v. Mukasey, 535 F.3d 962, 970 (9th Cir. 2008). California Rule of
 9   Professional Conduct 1.16(b) states that, subject to permission granted by a tribunal, counsel
10   “may withdraw from representing a client” for several enumerated reasons, including when, as
11   here, “(4) the client [by other conduct not enumerated in subsections 1 through 3]. . . renders it
12   unreasonably difficult for the lawyer to carry out the representation effectively,” or “(5) . . .
13   breaches a material term of an agreement with, or obligation, to the lawyer relating to the
14   representation,” and the lawyer has given the client a reasonable warning of withdrawal unless

15   the breach is cured. Cal. R. Prof Conduct 1.16(b)(4)-(5), 1.16(c).

16           Rule 3.1362(c) of the California Rules of Court provides that the declaration offered in

17   support of a motion to be relieved as counsel “must state in general terms and without

18   compromising the confidentiality of the attorney-client relationship,” but the disclosure must
     state no more than is necessary to substantiate a basis to withdraw. To this end, Formal Opinion
19
     2015-192 of the State Bar of California’s Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility
20
     and Conduct provides the following guidance of what lawyers may ethically disclose to the
21
     Court in connection with a motion to be relieved as counsel:
22
             An attorney may disclose to the court only as much as is reasonably necessary to
23           demonstrate her need to withdraw, and ordinarily it will be sufficient to say only
             words to the effect that ethical considerations require withdrawal or that there has
24           been an irreconcilable breakdown in the attorney-client relationship. In attempting
25           to demonstrate to the court her need to withdraw, an attorney may not disclose
             confidential communications with the client, either in open court or in camera.
26
     Cal. Bar Formal Op. 2015-192.
27
28
         NTC. OF MOT. TO WITHDRAW AS COUNSEL FOR DASAGROUP WITH MEMORANDUM
                                                        6          Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                   No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT            Document 147         Filed 09/17/25          Page 7 of 10


             In ruling on a motion for withdrawal, the courts consider “(1) the reasons counsel seeks
 1
     to withdraw; (2) the possible prejudice that withdrawal may cause to other litigants; (3) the harm
 2
     that withdrawal might cause to the administration of justice; and (4) the extent to which
 3
     withdrawal will delay resolution of the case.” Goldberg v. Teachbk, Inc, No. 24-cv-04525-LJC,
 4
     2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 89337, at *1-2 (N.D.Cal. May 9, 2025) (quoting Atkins v. Bank of Am.,
 5
     N.A., No. 15-cv-00051, 2015 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 89360, *2 (N.D.Cal. July 9, 2015)). “[T]he
 6
     consent of the client is not dispositive.” General Star Indem. Co. v. First Am. Title Ins. Co., 2021
 7
     U.S. Dist. LEXIS 50318, at *7 (N.D.Cal. Mar. 17, 2021) (quoting Robinson v. Delgado, 2010
 8
     U.S. Dist. LEXIS 92924, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 18, 2010)).
 9           In addition, counsel “shall not terminate a representation until the lawyer has taken
10   reasonable steps to avoid reasonably foreseeable prejudice to the rights of the client, such as
11   giving the client sufficient notice to permit the client to retain other counsel,” releasing all client
12   materials and property to the client upon termination, and refunding the client for any fee or
13   expense “paid in advance that the lawyer has not yet earned or incurred.” Cal. Prof. Conduct
14   Rule 1.16(d)-(e).

15               B.​ Leave to Withdraw is Appropriate Under the California Rules of
                     Professional Conduct.
16
             Withdrawal is appropriate under California Rules of Professional Conduct 1.16(b)(4) and
17
     (5), each of which individually and collectively establish good cause for allowing the
18
     undersigned counsel to withdraw from representing Dasagroup in this action.
19
             First, as noted in the accompanying declaration of counsel, Dasagroup has materially
20
     breached its representation agreement with its counsel. Despite being provided with notice and
21
     an opportunity to cure, Dasagroup has not cured this breach. See Moya Decl. ¶¶ 12-16. This
22
     material breach threatens considerable hardship to the undersigned law firm if it is forced to
23
     continue to represent Dasagroup through trial. Id. ¶¶ 16-17. This material breach is good cause
24   to grant counsel leave to withdraw. See, e.g., Morrow v. Mid Peninsula Hotels, LLC, 2020 U.S.
25   Dist. LEXIS 155277, at *2 (N.D.Cal. Aug. 26, 2020) (granting motion to withdraw filed by small
26   law firm whose corporate client’s nonpayment of legal fees threatened firm with financial
27   hardship); General Star Indem. Co. v. First Am. Title Ins. Co., 2021 U.S.Dist.LEXIS 50318, at *8
28
        NTC. OF MOT. TO WITHDRAW AS COUNSEL FOR DASAGROUP WITH MEMORANDUM
                                                        7           Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                    No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 147         Filed 09/17/25         Page 8 of 10


     (N.D.Cal. Mar. 17, 2021) (“A client's failure to pay legal fees constitutes good cause to permit an
 1
     attorney's withdrawal.”) (collecting cases); Kannan v. Apple Inc., 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 2308,
 2
     at *4 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 7, 2020) (granting motion to withdraw where litigant “has refused or failed
 3
     to pay costs and fees incurred during the past two and a half months”).
 4
            Second, as carefully noted in counsel’s declaration to avoid disclosure of privileged
 5
     matters and in compliance with State Bar Formal Opinion 2015-192, withdrawal is also
 6
     necessitated by a breakdown in the attorney-client relationship. See Moya Decl. ¶¶ 18-19. This
 7
     is also an independent basis for withdrawal. See Nob Hill Catering, Inc. v. Back of the House
 8
     LLC, 2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 237711, at *4 (N.D.Cal. Sep. 19, 2024) (granting motion to
 9   withdraw pursuant to RPC 1.16(b)(4) resulting from “a disagreement as to the overall strategy of
10   the case, issues with communication, and broken trust” and also granting motion, in part, because
11   the “the Court will not require counsel to work without compensation”); Perplexity Solved Sols.,
12   Inc. v. Perplexity AI, Inc., 2025 U.S.Dist.LEXIS 150757, at *3 (N.D.Cal. Aug. 5, 2025) (granting
13   motion to withdraw based on attestation by counsel of “a breakdown in the attorney-client
14   relationship such that her firm's continued representation of Plaintiff is unreasonably difficult”);

15   Max v. Hernandez, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 107157, *2-4 (S.D. Cal. Oct. 11, 2007) (granting

16   motion to withdraw based on counsel’s statement that “withdrawal is necessitated by a

17   breakdown in the attorney-client relationship due to disagreements regarding the best way to

18   proceed and Plaintiff's unwillingness to follow . . . advice”).
                C.​ Withdrawal Will Not Prejudice Other Litigants, Will Not Harm the
19
                    Administration of Justice, and Will Not Delay the Resolution of the Case.
20
            The undersigned counsel have provided Dasagroup with reasonable notice of its intent to
21
     file a motion to withdraw from this case and it has complied with all notice requirements. See
22
     Cal. RPC 1.16(b)(5), (d); Civ. L. R. 11-5(a); Moya Decl. ¶¶ 15, 20; Certificate of Service.
23
            Counsel respectfully submits that said withdrawal of counsel will not prejudice other
24   parties, will not harm administration of justice, and will not delay resolution of the case. First,
25   there would be little prejudice to other litigants if this motion were granted because the trial date
26   in this matter is set for January 4, 2027, well over a year away. Even if there were a short stay of
27   the action while Dasagroup finds substitute counsel, this still provides ample time for the action
28
        NTC. OF MOT. TO WITHDRAW AS COUNSEL FOR DASAGROUP WITH MEMORANDUM
                                                       8          Jefferies Funding v. Dasagroup Holdings et al.
                                                                  No. 3:24-cv-05639-TLT
        Case 3:24-cv-05639-TLT           Document 147         Filed 09/17/25          Page 9 of 10


     to proceed thereafter with the current trial date, and no trial continuance will be necessary.
 1
     Moreover, Dasagroup’s CEO was only recently added to this lawsuit and has yet to enter an
 2
     appearance. Moya Decl. 10. Mr. Ward will likely need time to obtain counsel on his own
 3
     behalf, to respond to the FAC, and to protect his own interests. Thus, a brief continuance to
 4
     allow Dasagroup to obtain new counsel at this juncture would not prejudice the parties.
 5
            All other litigants in this case are represented by common counsel at Holland & Knight
 6
     and appear to be working in close coordination. Given that the current trial date in this action is
 7
     set for January 4, 2027, well more than one year away, there is ample time for Dasagroup to
 8
     substitute in new counsel without much disruption to opposing parties, who are presently
 9   represented in common. To date, there has only been one deposition of the defaulted party
10   London Fruit, and the parties have yet to take depositions of any employees, officers and
11   directors of the other parties to the action (i.e., Dasagroup, Silo and Jefferies). Moya Decl. ¶¶ 23
12          There is also likely little prejudice or delay because of the non-waivable challenge to
